newsitem.title: GERMANY: Signs of German tax compromise, new talks possible.
newsitem.headline: Signs of German tax compromise, new talks possible.

text.p: Signs that government coalition members and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) were nearing positions on a planned reform of Germany's tax system appeared on Wednesday.

The Cologne-based Express newspaper quoted SPD parliamentary business manager Peter Struck in an interview as saying he could accept a lowering of the top German income tax rate, part of a major tax reform Bonn wants to introduce.
Struck was quoted as saying he could accept a cut in the top tax rate from the current 53 percent to 45 percent.

The paper also quoted Rainer Bruederle, deputy chairman of the Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners and the most vocal supporters of tax cuts, as saying he was proposing a top tax rate of 41 percent.
Kohl's government has previously said it was seeking to cut the rate down to 39 percent while the SPD has insisted that cuts to the top rate were barely able to be financed.

FDP chief Wolfgang Gerhardt, asked to comment on Bruederle's proposal as he arrived in Bonn for coalition talks later on Wednesday on German finances, said only that "it would be good if it came down as much as possible".
The SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, in April pulled out of talks aimed at getting cross-party support for the reform.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel was reported in the mass circulation Bild newspaper to have renewed an offer to the SPD for further talks.

But, to the likely dismay of his FDP coalition partners, he was also said to have reaffirmed his insistence that tax rises could not yet be ruled out because of Germany's continued problems in striving to meet single European currency deficit criteria.
"Given the financial situation, the coalition should not from the start rule out ways of covering holes in the budget," he was quoted as saying.
